title: Hypersonic missiles highlight arms race on Korean Peninsula
summary: Both South and North Korea have tested weapons feared by military planners for their speed and ability to maneuver in flight.

image.caption: Hypersonic missiles are far harder for defenders to identify, track and destroy [FILE: January 6, 2022]Image: YONHAPNEWS AGENCY/picture alliance

blocks.text: North Korea announced that it had tested two types of submarine-launched cruise missiles off its east coast on Wednesday — a day after the state-run Korean Central News Agency reported that leader Kim Jong Un had visited a new defense industry museum, where he admired an intercontinental ballistic missile reportedly capable of hitting targets in the continental United States.
The visit came five days after South Korean President Lee Jae-myung observed the test launch of his country's first domestically developed hypersonic missile.

South Korea's breakthrough came after Pyongyang announced a test on October 3 of what it described as a hypersonic intermediate-range missile that traveled 350 kilometers (220 miles) before striking its target.

"Comrade Kim Jong Un expressed the expectation and belief that all the nation's missile forces would remain faithful to their missions of defending the sovereignty and security of the republic in a responsible combat posture," the KCNA reported.
'Advanced conventional weapons'
Both North and South Korea are primarily racing to develop hypersonic technology because it offers a step-up in offensive capabilities at a time of worsening tensions in the Indo-Pacific region.

blocks.caption: Pyongyang said it had tested two types of submarine-launched cruise missiles off its east coast on October 14Image: KCNA/REUTERS

blocks.text: Hypersonic missiles are weapons that can travel at velocities of at least five times the speed of sound (Mach 5) or over 6,100 kilometers per hour.

Their speed makes it far harder for defenders to identify, track and destroy inbound missiles, which can carry conventional or nuclear warheads. Their additional advantage over previous generations of missiles is their ability to suddenly change course, dip or weave in flight, making interception significantly more difficult.

"There has been an arms race on the Korean Peninsula for many years and hypersonic weapons are just the latest manifestation of that," said Chris Green, Korea Peninsula analyst for Crisis Group International.
Hypersonic weapons have become a "priority for the South" as the North has ramped up its capabilities and forged military and economic ties with Russia, he said.
"And North Korea has nuclear weapons, but it would not be viable to use them as the threat has always been that doing so would mean that the US would turn the country to glass," he told DW.
"For the North, it is unsurprising that the geopolitics of the region have encouraged them to pursue advanced conventional weapons as they try to have dominance on the peninsula."
What lessons is North Korea learning from the Iran war?
Pyongyang 'should not be underestimated'

And while it is impossible to confirm with any certainty that the weapons the North says it has developed have the capabilities they claim, Green said it would be a mistake to underestimate Pyongyang.

"We do not know their capabilities and it is possible this is all propaganda, but there is a long list of times the North's capabilities have been underestimated only to be shown that they can, in fact, do what they say."
Chun In-bum, a retired general in the South Korean army and now a senior fellow with the National Institute for Deterrence Studies, shares that assessment of the threat.
"It's anybody's guess whether they're telling the truth on this, but any prudent military planner should always assume the worst," he said.
The North's mastery of the advanced technology required to operate hypersonic missiles appears to have been sudden, although it remains unclear how it acquired the capability.

"They probably obtained the technology through illegal means," Chun said. "They snoop around firms in the US, South Korea and Japan for this sort of information, but they also do it to their 'friends.'"
Wherever the data came from, the fact that North Korea's hypersonic missiles appear to have performed as required should be cause for deep concern.

"A greater offensive capability increases the overall danger posed by the North, and if they have weapons that are harder to shoot down, then it is possible there are greater temptations to use them," Chun said.
"I'm speculating, of course, but I'm sure that we are looking at ways to neutralize this particular threat, but as I understand it there is no good answer right now," Chun added.
South Korea proposes talks to officially end war with North
Canceling each other out?
Green, however, believes that both sides developing viable systems means that they may cancel each other out as a potent battlefield advantage.

"I do not think this changes the balance of power," he said. "The North still has its nuclear deterrent and this 'porcupine strategy' of being sharp and prickly in order to keep everyone else at arm's length. And it's not a game changer south of the Demilitarized Zone either," the expert added.

"It is clear, however, that if the North continues to develop its offensive systems and is able to deploy them in huge numbers, then there will have to be a conversation about greater missile defense not only in the South but also in Japan, and that will then raise some very difficult questions."
